candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a very high malware probability (0.9999), and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with SHAP contributions from +0.0063 to +0.0169. The supplied evidence does not independently support a high-confidence call, though. Every n-gram has a reported relative frequency of 0.000000, and no function locations are listed, so none of the patterns can be tied to a specific routine, loop, or code region. Most of the n-grams are generic compiler-generated control-flow and data-movement idioms: TEST JZ, TEST JS, CMP JL, MOV JZ, PUSH SUB, SUB MOV, AND MOV, LEA CALL, CALL ADD, CALL XOR, ADD POP, SUB LEA, MOV LEA. These appear in nearly all compiled x86 code and are not specific to mining. A few patterns are somewhat more suggestive of bitwise or arithmetic-heavy code: XOR XOR, XOR SHL, XOR MOV, XOR CALL, and XOR CMOVNZ. The conditional-move patterns CMOVZ MOV and CMP CMOVZ (the top two contributors) suggest branchless selection. XOR/shift sequences and branchless logic are consistent with hashing or cipher-style routines, but they also occur in ordinary code such as checksums, PRNGs, and compression. The evidence contains no mining-specific indicators in the form of recognizable constants, function names, or API usage. The classification therefore rests mainly on the aggregate model output, not on interpretable behavior. The result is that some indicators are present but inconclusive.
